verdict.summary:
ELECTRON MASS — 2024 PDG REVIEW OF PARTICLE PHYSICS (S. Navas et al., Particle Data Group, Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024))

1. THE ANSWER (both printed values, verbatim, with parenthetical uncertainties)

    m_e = 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c^2
        = 9.109 383 7015(28) x 10^-31 kg

    Fractional uncertainty printed in the source's last column: 0.30 ppb (i.e. 3.0 x 10^-10 relative).

    Where it is printed:
      - Review of Particle Physics 2024, "Physical Constants" review (rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf), Table 1.1, row "electron mass  m_e".
      - Same table reproduced in the 2024 Particle Physics Booklet (db2024.pdf), Table 1.1, row "electron mass".
      - Both copies carry the identical digits, so the choice between the Booklet and the full Review does not affect this value.

2. HOW TO READ THE PARENTHESES (needed to enter the value in a spreadsheet)

    PDG convention (stated in the table caption): the digits in parentheses are the 1-sigma uncertainty in the last printed digits of the value.

      MeV/c^2 :  0.510 998 950 00 (15)  ->  (0.510 998 950 00 +/- 0.000 000 000 15) MeV/c^2
                 i.e. 0.510 998 950 00 +/- 1.5 x 10^-10 MeV/c^2

      kg      :  9.109 383 7015 (28) x 10^-31  ->  (9.109 383 7015 +/- 0.000 000 0028) x 10^-31 kg
                 i.e. 9.109 383 7015 x 10^-31 +/- 2.8 x 10^-40 kg

    Self-consistency of the two printings (both reduce to the same 0.30 ppb):
      1.5e-10 / 0.51099895000 = 2.94e-10  = 0.29 ppb   -> rounds to 0.30 ppb  [OK]
      2.8e-40 / 9.1093837015e-31 = 3.07e-10 = 0.31 ppb   -> consistent with 0.30 ppb  [OK]

    Cross-check that the two printed values are the same mass (using constants from the same 2024 PDG table):
      u = 931.494 102 42(28) MeV/c^2 = 1.660 539 066 60(50) x 10^-27 kg
      => 1 MeV/c^2 = 1.66053906660e-27 / 931.49410242 = 1.782 661 92 x 10^-30 kg
      0.510 998 950 00 x 1.78266192e-30 = 9.109 38 x 10^-31 kg   -> agrees with the printed 9.109 383 7015e-31 kg  [OK]

3. SPREADSHEET ENTRY RECIPE (detector-calibration use)

    Use four columns, not one — this is what prevents the two classic errors (silent unit conversion and lost trailing zeros):

      Column A  quantity        : "electron mass"
      Column B  value           : 0.51099895000          (numeric, 11 decimal places)
      Column C  stat. unc.      : 1.5E-10                 (numeric, 1-sigma, absolute, same unit as B)
      Column D  unit            : "MeV/c^2"
      Column E  source          : "PDG 2024, Table 1.1 (Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001)"

      Second row (the kg printing, kept as a separate record rather than a formula):
      Column A  : "electron mass"
      Column B  : 9.1093837015E-31
      Column C  : 2.8E-40
      Column D  : "kg"
      Column E  : "PDG 2024, Table 1.1 (Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001)"

    Practical notes:
      - Enter the MeV/c^2 value as a NUMBER, not as the string "0.510 998 950 00(15)"; spreadsheets cannot do arithmetic on the parenthesis form. Keep the verbatim printed string in a comment/notes cell if traceability matters.
      - Do NOT let the spreadsheet display-format to fewer decimals. 0.51099895000 has 11 decimal places; a default "General" format will show 0.511 and silently destroy the precision. Set the cell format explicitly (e.g. 0.00000000000).
      - Do NOT type the kg value as a formula "=B1*1.78266192E-30". Enter the PDG-printed kg value directly (as assumed in the request) and, if you want a check, put the conversion in a separate audit cell and compare — they agree to all printed digits.
      - Unit column must read "MeV/c^2" (mass), not "MeV" (energy). PDG also lists the mass energy equivalent m_e c^2 = 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV — same digits, different dimension. If the calibration formula uses E = m c^2 with m in kg, use the kg row; if it uses momenta in MeV/c, use the MeV/c^2 row. Never mix the two rows inside one expression.

4. CAVEATS AND SCOPE (state these next to the cell, not in it)

    - The 2024 PDG constants table is built on CODATA 2018 (Tiesinga et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 93, 025010 (2021); NIST SP961). The review itself carries the footnote: values reflecting the 2022 CODATA set, released online in May 2024, "will be incorporated in future editions of the Review." Therefore the value above is the correct 2024-edition printing, and a later PDG edition may differ in the last digits. Pin the edition in the spreadsheet ("PDG 2024") and re-verify if you upgrade.
    - The 2024 edition is "an updating through January 2024"; cite it as S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024).
    - 0.30 ppb is far below any detector-calibration sensitivity; for essentially all calibration work the uncertainty on m_e is negligible and the practical risk is unit/roundoff mishandling, not the uncertainty itself. Preserve the printed uncertainty anyway, as requested, so the spreadsheet stays traceable to the source.
    - If other constants (c, e, h, hbar c, alpha, r_e) are used in the same calibration, take them from the same 2024 PDG Table 1.1 so the set is internally consistent with this mass value.

5. NOT DONE / OUT OF SCOPE FOR ME

    Nothing in the four asks is blocked; both numbers are read directly off the fetched 2024 PDG pages. What I cannot do from here is confirm which physical artifact the requester has in hand (printed Book, Booklet, or the PDF/online table). That does not change the answer for the electron mass, since the Booklet Table 1.1 and the full "Physical Constants" review print identical digits for this row.

intrinsic spatial extensions of the sources. It is also clearly shown that the sources are divided into
two groups: Galactic and extragalactic.

Cosmic rays (CRs) are a non-thermal population of particles that
pervade the Universe. Their salient characteristics can be inferred from
their major observational properties: spectrum, composition and arrival
directions. For charged CRs, the energies extend from tens of MeV to
close to 1 ZeV, the flux is ∼ 104 m−2
s−1
sr−1 above 1 GeV, but the dif-ferential spectrum falls steeply with energy E, following a power-law
dependence E−γ. The most striking spectral features are the “knee” at
a few PeV where the spectral index γ changes from ∼ 2.7 to ∼ 3, the
“second knee” at ∼ 100 PeV with a change to ∼ 3.3 and the “ankle” at a
few EeV where γ changes to ∼ 2.5. The flux is largely suppressed above a
few tens of EeV. Charged CRs are composed mostly of protons, helium,
and other nuclei, as well as electrons, positrons and anti-protons. In
the detection of CRs, two classes of techniques are distinguished: direct
observations, making use of the interactions of CRs in particle physics

results on mass, coupling, and the discovery

The Telescope Array (TA) experiment is a hybrid observatory designed to study ultra-high energy
cosmic rays (UHECRs). As the largest UHECR observatory in the Northern Hemisphere, the
TA experiment covers a 700 km2
area on the ground in Millard County, Utah, USA. The TA
surface detector (SD) consists of 507 plastic scintillation counters arranged on a square grid
with 1.2 km spacing. Furthermore, the skies over the array are viewed by three fluorescence
detector (FD) stations positioned around its periphery, which observe the development of cosmic
ray showers in the atmosphere. Over the past 16 years, the TA experiment has maintained stable
operation, ensuring data collection with high efficiency. This stability and high statistical precision
have allowed us to observe three distinct spectral breaks in the TA SD energy spectrum: ankle,
shoulder, and cutoff. In this presentation, we will report the latest TA SD energy spectrum and
update our findings on the anisotropy of the energy spectrum.

verdict.summary:
Source: Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics, 2024 edition, '30. Cosmic Rays' (S. Navas et al., Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024); review written October 2023).

Finding: The 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review defines ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) by an energy threshold of 10^18 eV, i.e. 1 EeV. The review expresses the boundary as cosmic rays 'above 10^18 eV.'

Inclusive/exclusive verdict: The threshold is exclusive. The wording 'above 10^18 eV' means E > 10^18 eV; a cosmic ray with energy exactly 10^18 eV is not included by the stated definition. If an inclusive convention were intended, the review would have to say 'at or above 10^18 eV' or 'E ≥ 10^18 eV,' which is not the wording used.

Important distinction: The review also mentions 'less than 1 particle per km^2 per year above 30 EeV' in its UHECR discussion. That 30 EeV figure is a flux benchmark, not the UHECR definition threshold, and must not be substituted for the 10^18 eV definition. Here 30 EeV = 3×10^19 eV.

Answer to ask 1: 10^18 eV (1 EeV).
Answer to ask 2: exclusive (E > 10^18 eV).

verdict.summary:
PRELIMINARY MARS-LANDER PRESSURE-MODEL INPUT, EXTRACTED FROM THE NASA MARS FACT SHEET

1. SOURCE AND SNAPSHOT CONTROL

Source page: NASA NSSDCA Mars Fact Sheet, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/marsfact.html
Curator: Dr. David R. Williams, NSSDCA, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center.
Page footer stamp on the captured copy: "Last Updated: 19 May 2025, DRW".
Capture: fetched 2026-11-23T11:49:10Z, sha256 366b0ce9b69c (harness fetch; page bytes as quoted in the grounding).

Snapshot validity for the requested date 2026-11-21: the page's own last-updated stamp (19 May 2025) precedes the requested date, and the capture was taken 2 days after it. The captured content is therefore the version in force on 2026-11-21, conditional only on the page having been edited between 2026-11-21 and 2026-11-23 without the footer stamp being refreshed. Record this as a traceability residual risk; it does not invalidate the extraction, and re-verification against a web archive capture dated 2026-11-21 is the single action that would close it.

2. VERBATIM SOURCE LINE (Martian Atmosphere block)

  "Surface pressure:  6.36 mb at mean radius (variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season)"
  "[6.9 mb to 9 mb (Viking 1 Lander site)]"

Three distinct quantities appear on these two lines and must not be conflated:
  (a) 6.36 mb  - the stated surface pressure at mean radius (the datum the model asks for).
  (b) 4.0 to 8.7 mb - the seasonal variability the sheet states for that same mean-radius datum. THIS is the seasonal range asked for.
  (c) 6.9 mb to 9 mb - a separate, site-specific bracketed figure for the Viking 1 Lander site, on a different (site elevation) datum. It is not the seasonal range and must not be substituted for it.

3. ANSWERED VALUES

Ask 1 - surface pressure at mean radius: 6.36 mb.
Ask 2 - stated seasonal range: 4.0 to 8.7 mb, "depending on season".

4. UNITS AND EXACT CONVERSIONS (for the pressure model)

The fact sheet states these in millibars (mb). Per the companion Fact Sheet Notes page, "Surface Pressure: Atmospheric pressure at the surface, in bars, millibars (mb = 10^-3 bar), or picobars". 1 mb = 1 hPa = 100 Pa = 0.001 bar.

  Mean-radius surface pressure:  6.36 mb  = 636 Pa   = 6.36 hPa  = 6.36e-3 bar
  Seasonal minimum:              4.0 mb   = 400 Pa   = 4.0 hPa   = 4.0e-3 bar
  Seasonal maximum:              8.7 mb   = 870 Pa   = 8.7 hPa   = 8.7e-3 bar
  Seasonal band width:           4.7 mb   = 470 Pa
  Ratio max/min:                 2.175

  (Sanity reference only, different datum - Viking 1 Lander site: 6.9 mb = 690 Pa to 9 mb = 900 Pa.)

Model-input convention: carry 636 Pa as the nominal value with a min/max band of 400 Pa / 870 Pa. Report in the sheet's native mb only if the model's unit field says so; otherwise use the Pa figures above. The conversions are exact powers of ten, so no rounding loss is introduced.

5. DATUM DEFINITION ('mean radius')

On the same fact sheet, "Volumetric mean radius (km) = 3389.5" for Mars; the Fact Sheet Notes define the volumetric mean radius as "Radius of a sphere with the same volume as the body" and define surface gravity (mean) as GM over the square of that volumetric mean radius. The pressure figure is therefore referenced to the 3389.5 km mean-radius sphere, i.e. a global zero-elevation reference - not to a landed site and not to the equatorial radius (3396.2 km). Consequences for the lander model, which the sheet itself makes explicit by bracketing the Viking figure: an actual landing site at high negative elevation (Hellas, Jezero, Gale floor) will read above the mean-radius value and a site on the southern highlands will read below it. The sheet's own site example, 6.9-9 mb at Viking 1, is +0.54 to +2.64 mb relative to 6.36 mb. Treat 636 Pa as a global datum input and scale to site elevation with a barometric relation using the sheet's own scale height (11.0 km) and mean molecular weight (43.49) before the value is used for structural or parachute loads.

6. CONSISTENCY CHECKS PERFORMED

- The nominal 6.36 mb lies strictly inside the stated 4.0-8.7 mb seasonal band (4.0 < 6.36 < 8.7). The deliverable's own numbers are mutually consistent.
- The Viking-site band (690-900 Pa) is entirely above the mean-radius nominal (636 Pa) and overlaps the upper part of the seasonal band (400-870 Pa). This is expected and is not a contradiction: it is a different elevation datum. It is labeled as such in the model input so it cannot be mistaken for the seasonal range.
- The general 'Planetary Fact Sheet - Metric' comparison table on the same NSSDCA site lists Mars Surface Pressure as "0.01" bars. That is 10 mb, i.e. a one-significant-figure rounding that disagrees with the Mars-specific sheet at the second significant figure. DO NOT use 0.01 bar as the model input; the Mars-specific fact sheet's 6.36 mb is the authoritative figure, and the Notes page warns generally that fact-sheet values are "based on ongoing research and as such are under study and subject to change at any time."
- Units: mb (millibar) is used consistently for both the nominal value and the seasonal range; no mixed-unit arithmetic appears above.

7. TRACEABILITY RECORD TO CARRY WITH THE MODEL INPUT

  Value: 636 Pa (6.36 mb) at 3389.5 km mean radius; band 400-870 Pa (4.0-8.7 mb) seasonal.
  Source: NASA NSSDCA Mars Fact Sheet, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/marsfact.html
  Version stamp: "Last Updated: 19 May 2025, DRW"; capture 2026-11-23T11:49:10Z, sha256 366b0ce9b69c.
  Companion definitions: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/fact_notes.html (Atmospheres section; volumetric mean radius definition).
  Status: preliminary, replaceable by mission-specific data (MOLA/MGS-M-MOLA-3-PEDR-L1A-V1.0 topography plus in-situ surface pressure measurements) before CDR-level load definition.

Distance from Sun (106 km or 106 miles) - This is the average distance from
the planet to the Sun in millions of kilometers or millions of miles, also known as the semi-major axis.
All planets have orbits which are elliptical, not perfectly circular, so there is a point in the orbit at
which the planet is closest to the Sun, the perihelion, and a point furthest from the Sun, the aphelion.
The average distance from the Sun is midway between these two values.  The average distance from the Earth
to the Sun is defined as 1 Astronomical Unit (AU), so the ratio table gives this distance in AU.
* For the Moon, the average distance from the Earth is given.

quotes.whole:
planet.
With no solid surface to slow them down, Jupiter’s spots can
persist for many years. The Great Red Spot, a swirling oval of
clouds twice as wide as Earth, has been observed on the gi-ant planet for more than 300 years. More recently, three smaller
ovals merged to form the Little Red Spot, about half the size of
its larger cousin. Scientists do not yet know if these ovals and
planet-circling bands are shallow or deeply rooted to the interior.
The composition of Jupiter’s atmosphere is similar to that of the
Sun — mostly hydrogen and helium. Deep in the atmosphere,
pressure and temperature increase, compressing the hydrogen
gas into a liquid. This gives Jupiter the largest ocean in the solar
system — an ocean made of hydrogen instead of water. Scien-tists think that, at depths perhaps halfway to the planet’s center,
the pressure becomes so great that electrons are squeezed off
the hydrogen atoms, making the liquid electrically conducting.
Jupiter’s fast rotation is thought to drive electrical currents in
this region, generating the planet’s powerful magnetic field. It is
still unclear if, deeper down, Jupiter has a central core of solid
material.

verdict.summary:
Source and date check
- Target source: NASA NSSDCA Jupiter Fact Sheet, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/jupiterfact.html (the page titled 'Jupiter Fact Sheet').
- Date evidence for the 'as available on 2026-11-21' constraint: the NSSDCA fact-sheet index page (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/index.html) states 'Last Updated: 13 November 2026'. The Jupiter Fact Sheet page was fetched 2026-11-23T11:51:43Z (sha256 9ac7835ae538). Because the last-updated stamp is 13 November 2026, before 2026-11-21, and no later update is indicated, the fetched values are the values in effect on 2026-11-21. This is an inference from the page's last-updated stamp; no separate Wayback capture dated 2026-11-21 was supplied.

Exact source text, from the 'Jovian Atmosphere' block of the Jupiter Fact Sheet:

    Surface Pressure: >>1000 bars
    Temperature at 1 bar: 165 K (-108 C)
    Temperature at 0.1 bar: 112 K (-161 C)
    Density at 1 bar: 0.16 kg/m3

Reported values:

| Pressure level | Kelvin as printed | Celsius as printed | Consistency check |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1 bar | 165 K | -108 C | 165 - 273.15 = -108.15 C, printed as -108 C |
| 0.1 bar | 112 K | -161 C | 112 - 273.15 = -161.15 C, printed as -161 C |

Both Celsius values are printed on the fact sheet alongside the kelvin values; they are not derived values. The conversion check above is only a consistency check and agrees with the sheet's integer-rounded Celsius figures.

Source-selection note: the general NSSDCA 'Planetary Fact Sheet - Metric' gives Jupiter 'Mean Temperature (C)' as -110 and 'Surface Pressure (bars)' as 'Unknown*'; it does not give a 0.1-bar temperature. That table is not the source used here because the request asks for the 1-bar and 0.1-bar entries, which appear on the detailed Jupiter Fact Sheet.

Final answer: at 1 bar the NASA Jupiter Fact Sheet lists 165 K (-108 C); at 0.1 bar it lists 112 K (-161 C).

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

In the abstract of Planck 2018 Results. VI. Cosmological parameters (Planck Collaboration, A&A 641, A6 (2020); arXiv:1807.06209), the Hubble constant inferred for the base-ΛCDM model from the Planck data alone, i.e. TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing, is

    H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km s^-1 Mpc^-1   (68% confidence)

Equivalently, at the full precision printed in Table 2 of the same paper for the same data combination, H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km s^-1 Mpc^-1. The two are the same constraint at different rounding (67.36 -> 67.4; 0.54 -> 0.5). The uncertainty quoted is the 68% (1σ) marginalized credible interval from the Monte Carlo chains; the unit is km s^-1 Mpc^-1 (= km/s/Mpc), and H0 = 100 h km s^-1 Mpc^-1, i.e. h ≈ 0.674.

WHAT THE ANSWER IS AND IS NOT

- Model: base-ΛCDM — spatially flat, six parameters (Ωbh^2, Ωch^2, 100θ_MC, τ, ln(10^10 A_s), n_s), power-law adiabatic scalar spectrum, no tensor modes, no extra relativistic species, no running, no curvature.
- Data: Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing (Planck 2018 final full-mission likelihoods: plikHM TT,TE,EE + lowl + lowE + the lensing reconstruction). This is the combination the abstract's base-ΛCDM statement refers to. No BAO, no supernovae, no local H0 prior.
- Nature of the number: H0 is a *derived* parameter in this fit, not a direct measurement. It follows from the angular scale of the acoustic peaks (θ_MC, measured to ~0.03%) together with the sound horizon at recombination, which is fixed by the pre-recombination physics constrained by the same spectra; this is why the Planck CMB value is model-dependent and why it sits below local distance-ladder values.

CROSS-CHECK TABLE (same paper, base-ΛCDM, for disambiguation — these are NOT the abstract value)

| Data combination                    | H0 (km s^-1 Mpc^-1) | Why it is not the answer |
|-------------------------------------|---------------------|--------------------------|
| TT,TE,EE+lowE                       | 67.27 ± 0.60         | lensing reconstruction not included |
| TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing               | 67.36 ± 0.54         | THIS is the abstract's combination (rounds to 67.4 ± 0.5) |
| TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO           | 67.66 ± 0.42         | an extension of the dataset, not base-ΛCDM Planck-alone |
| Riess18 (SHOES) prior, H0 = 73.45 ± 1.66 | (external input) | appears in the Planck parameter-table documentation as a *prior*, never as a Planck inference |
| Planck 2015 XIII                     | 67.8 ± 0.9           | previous release, wrong paper |

Ordering check: 67.27 < 67.36 < 67.66 and the errors shrink 0.60 -> 0.54 -> 0.42 as data are added, as expected; the headline 67.4 ± 0.5 is consistent with, not in conflict with, any row above.

VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (one minute, if the wording must be quoted verbatim)

1. Open https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209 (v3, 14 Sep 2020, is the version matching the A&A publication, DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201833910).
2. Read the abstract block only. Locate the sentence that introduces the base-ΛCDM results ('... the base-ΛCDM model ...'); it is there that H0 is quoted with its uncertainty.
3. Confirm three things in that sentence: (a) the model tag is base-ΛCDM; (b) the data combination is the Planck-only TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing set, with no '+BAO' and no external H0 prior; (c) the quoted number is 67.4 ± 0.5 (abstract rounding) or 67.36 ± 0.54 (full precision). Either way the reported value and uncertainty of this deliverable stand.
4. Cross-check against Table 2 (base-ΛCDM, column 'TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing'): H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54, Ωm = 0.3153 ± 0.0073.

RESIDUAL RISK / SCOPE NOTE

The source passages available to me confirm the paper's identity and bibliographic record but do not reproduce the abstract's text, so the value above rests on the paper's established published content rather than on a quoted passage. The only wording-level uncertainty is whether the abstract prints '67.4 ± 0.5' or the table-precision '67.36 ± 0.54'; both are given above, they are the same constraint, and step 2-3 of the procedure resolves which string to copy. The physics answer — H0 ≈ 67.4 ± 0.5 km s^-1 Mpc^-1 for base-ΛCDM from Planck alone — is unaffected.

asks.quote: the equatorial-minus-polar radius difference
in km

verdict.summary:
EQUATORIAL-MINUS-POLAR RADIUS DIFFERENCE

Given (NASA Earth Fact Sheet):
  a (equatorial radius) = 6378.137 km
  b (polar radius)      = 6356.752 km

Computation (signed, equatorial minus polar):
  Δr = a − b = 6378.137 km − 6356.752 km = 21.385 km

Worked column arithmetic:
      6378.137
    − 6356.752
    ----------
  thousandths: 7 − 2 = 5
  hundredths:  3 − 5  -> borrow 1 from tenths (0 becomes 10 via borrow chain), 13 − 5 = 8
  tenths:      0 − 7  -> borrow 1 from units, 10 − 7 = 3
  units:       7 − 6 = 1   (7 after the borrow from 8)
  tens:        7 − 5 = 2
  hundreds:    3 − 3 = 0
  thousands:   6 − 6 = 0
  Result: 21.385 km

Verification (inverse operation):
  6356.752 + 21.385 = 6378.137 ✓

Sign and precision:
  - The result is positive because the equatorial radius exceeds the polar radius, as required for an oblate spheroid; a negative value would indicate transposed operands.
  - Both operands are quoted to three decimal places (0.001 km), so the difference is exact at that precision; no rounding is applied. Report as 21.385 km (21.4 km if a tenth-of-a-km figure is preferred).

Independent cross-check via flattening:
  f = (a − b)/a = 21.385 / 6378.137 = 0.0033528 ≈ 1/298.26
  This matches the accepted Earth flattening (1/298.257), confirming the operands are in the correct order and the subtraction is sound.

Answer: 21.385 km.
Spacecraft mass-budget percentage calculation; medium-risk, reversible audit arithmetic.

asks.quote: what percentage of the launch mass was propellant?
Round to one decimal place.

verdict.summary:
Mass-budget audit — Gaia propellant mass fraction

1. Inputs (from the ESA Gaia factsheet as quoted in the request)
   - Launch mass (wet mass, at liftoff): m_launch = 2030 kg
   - Propellant mass: m_prop = 400 kg
   - Relation: the 400 kg of propellant is INCLUDED IN the 2030 kg launch mass, i.e. m_prop is a subset of m_launch, not additive to it.

2. Formula
   Propellant percentage = (m_prop / m_launch) x 100

3. Calculation (full precision)
   m_prop / m_launch = 400 / 2030 = 0.197044334975...
   x 100 = 19.7044334975... %

4. Rounding
   Requirement: round to one decimal place.
   19.704433... % -> second decimal digit is 0 -> 19.7 %

5. Result
   Propellant accounted for 19.7 % of Gaia's launch mass.

6. Audit cross-checks
   - Subset/consistency: 400 kg <= 2030 kg, so the fraction is physically admissible (<= 100 %). The residual launch mass is 2030 - 400 = 1630 kg of non-propellant (dry) mass, i.e. 80.3 %; 19.7 % + 80.3 % = 100.0 %, so the budget closes.
   - Rounding closure: 19.7 % of 2030 kg = 400.31 kg versus the source value of 400 kg; the 0.31 kg deviation is purely the one-decimal rounding residue and does not violate any constraint.
   - Formatting constraint check: the reported value 19.7 is stated to exactly one decimal place.

7. Interpretation note (no alternative figure emitted)
   The computation assumes 'launch mass' means wet mass at liftoff (2030 kg total, propellant included), which matches the factsheet wording 'including 400 kg of propellant'. Under any other reading the question would be ill-posed; on this grounding the answer is 19.7 %.

verdict.summary:
Source selection and quoted values (NASA NSSDCA Planetary Fact Sheets):

- Earth Fact Sheet (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html), Last Updated 15 November 2024: under 'Terrestrial Atmosphere', 'Surface pressure: 1014 mb'. This is the listed Earth surface pressure. (1014 mb = 101,400 Pa.)
- Mars Fact Sheet (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html), Last Updated 19 May 2025: under 'Martian Atmosphere', 'Surface pressure: 6.36 mb at mean radius (variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season)'. The mean-radius value 6.36 mb is used; the seasonal 4.0-8.7 mb range is explicitly excluded. (6.36 mb = 636 Pa.)

Date check: both detail sheets carry Last Updated dates before 2026-11-21, and the fetched copies (2026-11-23) show those same lines, so these are the values listed as available on 2026-11-21.

Calculation:
Earth pressure / Mars pressure = 1014 mb / 6.36 mb = 101400 Pa / 636 Pa = 159.433962264...
The units cancel, so the ratio is dimensionless.
Rounding to one decimal place: 159.433962264... -> 159.4. The second decimal digit is 3, so there is no tie; round-half-up and round-half-even agree.

Result: 159.4

Notes:
- The generic 'Planetary Fact Sheet - Metric' table lists Earth 1 bar and Mars 0.01 bar. Those are heavily rounded table entries and do not carry the Mars mean-radius value. The request's 'at mean radius' points to the Mars detail sheet, so the detail-sheet values above are used.
- Do not use 1013.25 mb (a common standard-atmosphere figure). The NASA Earth fact sheet as fetched lists 1014 mb; using 1013.25 would give 159.3, which is not the fact-sheet-listed value.
- Do not use Mars seasonal extremes: 4.0 mb would give 253.5 and 8.7 mb would give 116.6; neither is the requested mean-radius comparison.

verdict.summary:
## 1. Answer

Per NASA's errata sheet for NTRS 19770009539 (*U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976*):

- **Enter S = 110.4 K.** (The document's Table 2, Category II Constants, footnote 3 prints `S = 110 K`.)
- **The document's value was too small by 0.4 K** (0.4 kelvin, an additive shortfall, *not* a factor; 110 + 0.4 = 110.4).

Relative shortfall: 0.4/110 = 0.36 %. Resulting error in computed dynamic viscosity: 0.4/(T + 110.4) ≈ **0.10 % at 288.15 K**, growing to ≈0.13 % at 200 K and shrinking to ≈0.04 % at 1000 K.

## 2. Source and exact wording

Errata sheet distributed with NTRS 19770009539 (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19770009539/downloads/19770009539.pdf), authored by Yekta Gursel, Ph.D., dated Thursday, January 08, 2015, addressed to NASA HQ-STI-INFODESK, subject "Re: NASA STI Order D-30869". Item 2 under "the rest of the errors I have found in Table 2, B. Category II Constants, on Page 2":

> "2) The value for Sutherland's constant S is too small by 0.4. It should be 110.4 Kelvin."

The document text being corrected (Table 2, footnote 3, page 2):

> "The Sutherland constant, S = 110 K, (Hilsenrath et al., 1955) is a constant in the empirical expression for dynamic viscosity."

The formula the constant belongs to (same footnote block; β = 1.458e-6 kg/(s·m·K^1/2)):

    μ = β · T^(3/2) / (T + S)

Corroboration that 110.4 K is the physically correct value (the printed 110 K is a truncation): the document's own cited source, Hilsenrath et al. (1955), gives 110.4 K; the MATLAB Aerospace Blockset ISA Atmosphere Model documents `S — Sutherland temperature, 110.4 K (default)`; COMSOL's table lists Air S = 111 K (rounded). The errata correction is therefore consistent with independent references and should be adopted without further justification.

**Scope note — do not conflate errata items.** The same errata sheet lists four other, unrelated defects: (a) R* on page 2 Table 2 differs from R* on page 3 by a factor of 10^6 (page 3 value is correct); (b) r0 (Earth mean radius) too large by 1000 in km; (c) sigma (mean effective collision diameter) too large by 10^9 in m; (d) Table III thermal-conductivity column 8 too small by 1000 (equation 53 itself is correct). This change request concerns **item (2), S only**. Items (a), (b), (c), (d) are separate defect tickets; if the same code hard-codes any of those constants, raise them separately rather than folding them into this patch.

## 3. Unit handling — how S must be entered

S is an *absolute temperature* in the Sutherland denominator and must be entered in the same temperature scale used for T in the code. It is independent of the viscosity unit system (SI vs cgs vs English); only β carries the viscosity units.

| Code temperature scale | Enter S as | Shortfall was | β (for reference) |
|---|---|---|---|
| K (SI; β = 1.458e-6 kg/(s·m·K^1/2)) | **110.4 K** | **0.4 K** | 1.458e-6 kg/(s·m·K^1/2) |
| K with cgs viscosity (g/(cm·s) = P) | 110.4 K | 0.4 K | 1.458e-5 g/(cm·s·K^1/2) |
| °R (English; μ in lb/(ft·s)) | **198.72 °R** (110.4 × 1.8) | **0.72 °R** (0.4 × 1.8) | 7.3034e-7 lb/(ft·s·°R^1/2) |
| °C | invalid — S is absolute | — | — |

Do **not** convert S by a viscosity factor. A 10×/1000× "fix" is wrong here; the errata says the shortfall is 0.4, an additive amount, and that the correct value is 110.4.

## 4. Code change

### 4.1 Constant definition (primary edit)

```diff
--- a/atmosphere/constants.py
+++ b/atmosphere/constants.py
@@
-# Sutherland constant, U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976, Table 2, Cat. II, p.2
-SUTHERLAND_S = 110.0        # K
+# Sutherland constant, U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976, Table 2, Cat. II, p.2.
+# The printed 110 K is too small by 0.4 K; corrected per the NASA NTRS
+# 19770009539 errata sheet (item 2): S = 110.4 K.
+# Source: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19770009539/downloads/19770009539.pdf
+SUTHERLAND_S = 110.4        # K  (errata: was 110 K, too small by 0.4 K)
```

If the constant is a configuration value rather than a literal, change the shipped default the same way:

```diff
- sutherland_temperature: 110.0   # K
+ sutherland_temperature: 110.4   # K  (NTRS 19770009539 errata item 2)
```

If the code carries °R internally:

```diff
- SUTHERLAND_S_R = 198.0     # deg R  (== 110.0 K)
+ SUTHERLAND_S_R = 198.72    # deg R  (== 110.4 K, per NTRS 19770009539 errata item 2)
```

### 4.2 Guard so the change is auditable and idempotent

```python
# atmosphere/viscosity.py
from .constants import SUTHERLAND_S, BETA

_ERRATA_S_K = 110.4  # NTRS 19770009539 errata, item 2
assert abs(SUTHERLAND_S - _ERRATA_S_K) < 1e-9, (
    f"Sutherland S = {SUTHERLAND_S} K does not match the errata value "
    f"{_ERRATA_S_K} K; see NTRS 19770009539 errata sheet, item 2."
)

def dynamic_viscosity(T):
    """Sutherland dynamic viscosity, US Std Atm 1976.
    mu = beta * T**1.5 / (T + S), T in K, S = 110.4 K (errata-corrected).
    """
    return BETA * T**1.5 / (T + SUTHERLAND_S)
```

If the code uses the reference-state form `μ = μ_ref (T/T_ref)^1.5 (T_ref + S)/(T + S)`, only S changes; μ_ref = 1.716e-5 kg/(m·s) at T_ref = 273.15 K is unaffected.

## 5. Verification

Post-change regression values from `μ = 1.458e-6 · T^1.5 / (T + 110.4)` (kg/(m·s)). Tolerance 1e-9 relative; these are closed-form, not measured.

| T (K) | μ, S = 110.4 K (new) | μ, S = 110 K (old) | Δμ | Δrel |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 200.00 | 1.328558e-5 | 1.330272e-5 | +1.71e-8 | 0.129 % |
| 216.65 | 1.421653e-5 | 1.423389e-5 | +1.74e-8 | 0.122 % |
| 288.15 | 1.789386e-5 | 1.791185e-5 | +1.80e-8 | 0.100 % |
| 500.00 | 2.691070e-5 | 2.692968e-5 | +1.90e-8 | 0.070 % |
| 1000.00 | 4.152727e-5 | 4.154234e-5 | +1.51e-8 | 0.036 % |

Sea-level sanity check: μ(288.15 K) = 1.7894e-5 kg/(m·s), matching the standard sea-level value quoted in the 1976 atmosphere tables (1.7894e-5). The old value gave 1.7912e-5, i.e. 0.10 % high.

English-unit check: μ(518.67 °R) = 7.3034e-7 × 518.67^1.5 / (518.67 + 198.72) = 1.2027e-5 lb/(ft·s), which equals 1.7894e-5 kg/(m·s) × 0.671969 — the two unit paths agree, confirming S = 198.72 °R is the correct entry in that system.

Test to add:

```python
def test_sutherland_constant_is_errata_corrected():
    assert SUTHERLAND_S == 110.4          # K

def test_viscosity_at_sea_level():
    assert abs(dynamic_viscosity(288.15) - 1.789386e-5) < 1e-11

def test_viscosity_monotonic_and_positive():
    ts = [200.0, 216.65, 288.15, 500.0, 1000.0]
    mus = [dynamic_viscosity(t) for t in ts]
    assert all(m > 0 for m in mus)
    assert all(b > a for a, b in zip(mus, mus[1:]))
```

## 6. Regression impact and re-baselining

- Every output that consumes dynamic viscosity shifts by at most ≈0.13 % (largest at the cold tropopause, smallest aloft); density, pressure and temperature are unaffected because S enters only the viscosity/conductivity branch.
- Reynolds number scales as 1/μ, so Re shifts by ≈0.10 % at sea level. Any stored baseline that asserts Re, drag, boundary-layer height or convective coefficient to tighter than 0.2 % must be re-baselined; tolerances looser than 0.2 % will pass unchanged.
- Kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ shifts by the same relative amount.
- Do **not** touch the thermal-conductivity Sutherland constant in the same edit. Its constant is a separate quantity (the errata's thermal-conductivity finding concerns Table III scaling by 1000, not S_k); changing it would be an unrequested behaviour change.

## 7. Change-record text

> Correct Sutherland constant S from 110 K to 110.4 K in the atmosphere viscosity model. The printed value in U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976 (NASA NTRS 19770009539), Table 2, Category II Constants, footnote 3, is too small by 0.4 K per the errata sheet distributed with that NTRS record (item 2: "The value for Sutherland's constant S is too small by 0.4. It should be 110.4 Kelvin."). Effect: dynamic and kinematic viscosity increase by 0.04–0.13 % over 200–1000 K (0.10 % at sea level); Reynolds-number baselines within 0.2 % are unaffected.

asks.quote: What corrected kt should be used, in J/(m·s·K)
what is the same value in W/(m·K)?

verdict.summary: Correction: The printed U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976, Table III value at 0 m geometric altitude is kt_printed = 2.5362 × 10^-5 J/(m·s·K). NASA's errata states this entry is too small by a factor of 1000, so the corrected value is kt_corrected = kt_printed × 1000 = 2.5362 × 10^-5 × 10^3 = 2.5362 × 10^-2 J/(m·s·K) = 0.025362 J/(m·s·K). Unit conversion: 1 J/(m·s·K) = 1 (J/s)/(m·K) = 1 W/(m·K). Therefore the same value in W/(m·K) is 2.5362 × 10^-2 W/(m·K) = 0.025362 W/(m·K). The numeric value is unchanged because the units are dimensionally identical. This is consistent with the expected thermal conductivity of air at sea level, approximately 0.025 W/(m·K), whereas the uncorrected printed value would be about 2.5 × 10^-5 W/(m·K), three orders of magnitude too small. Report the corrected value to the same five significant figures as the printed entry: 2.5362 × 10^-2 J/(m·s·K), or equivalently 2.5362 × 10^-2 W/(m·K).

verdict.summary:
# Verdict and stated region

**Ask 1 — Does the stated validity region of Eq. (34.5) support evaluating it at βγ = 0.01 and claiming the review's few-percent accuracy?  →  NO.**

**Ask 2 — βγ region over which the review states that accuracy:  0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000**  (dimensionless; both limits are stated by the review to be Z-dependent).

βγ = 0.01 lies one full decade *below* the stated lower bound. It is outside the region, not at its edge.

---

## 1. Primary source, quoted verbatim

From *34. Passage of Particles Through Matter*, in S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D **110**, 030001 (2024), p. 5, immediately following Eq. (34.5):

> "Eq. (34.5) is valid in the region 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000 with an accuracy of a few percent. At βγ ∼ 0.1 the projectile speed is comparable to atomic electron "speed," and at βγ ∼ 1000 radiative effects begin to be important (Sec. 34.6). Both limits are Z dependent. A minor dependence on M at high energies is introduced through Wmax, but for all practical purposes the stopping power in a given material is a function of β alone. Small corrections are discussed in Sec. 34.2.6."

**Provenance.** Two independently fetched copies of the same review agree word-for-word on this sentence:

| Copy | Footer date | sha256 (prefix) |
|---|---|---|
| `pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf` | 25th March, 2025 | `1b328278e835` |
| `pdg.lbl.gov/2026/download/rpp-2025/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf` | 31st May, 2024 | `3ead731273e0` |

The edition ambiguity raised in the plan is therefore **closed**: the accuracy statement is identical in both dated renderings, so the verdict does not depend on which one the analyst reads.

**Rendering note (disclosed, not glossed).** The PDF text layer extracts the relation as a period — "0.1 . βγ . 1000". That glyph is PDG's *≲* (lesssim: "approximately less than or of order"), not a strict inequality and not a multiplication dot. I have restored ≲ above and it should be quoted that way. The softness is an order-of-magnitude caveat *at the edge* of the interval; it cannot stretch a bound of 0.1 down to 0.01. The answer is insensitive to whether one reads the bound as strict or soft.

---

## 2. Why the answer is No — from the review's own sentences

The quoted passage excludes the proposed use three separate ways, and any one of them is sufficient:

1. **Categorical.** 0.01 < 0.1. The formula's validity interval is stated to begin at 0.1; βγ = 0.01 is a decade below it.
2. **Physical, in the review's own justification.** The review grounds the lower bound as the point where "the projectile speed is comparable to atomic electron 'speed.'" At βγ = 0.01 (β = 0.0099995) the projectile is ten times slower still — deep in the adiabatic / strong-coupling regime, where the first Born approximation on which Eq. (34.5) rests is not merely inaccurate but inapplicable (§3 below quantifies this).
3. **The escape hatch does not reach.** The only extension offered is "Small corrections are discussed in Sec. 34.2.6." At βγ = 0.01 the corrections to the Bethe form (shell, Barkas–Andersen, Bloch, effective charge / charge state, nuclear stopping) are O(10–100 %) — they are not small corrections, they are the physics.

Note also that the review says **"Both limits are Z dependent."** Whoever quotes the interval must carry that qualifier: the 0.1 lower bound is not a universal constant, it shifts with the material. But no Z shifts it down to 0.01.

---

## 3. Quantitative check at βγ = 0.01

### 3.1 Kinematics

With βγ = 0.01: β = 0.00999950, γ = 1.0000500, β² = 9.9990 × 10⁻⁵, **β²γ² = 1.0000 × 10⁻⁴**.

Maximum energy transfer in PDG Eq. (34.5), W_max = 2m_ec²β²γ² / (1 + 2γm_e/M + (m_e/M)²):

- proton: **W_max = 102.1 eV**
- corresponding kinetic energies: p 46.9 keV, μ 5.28 keV, π 6.98 keV.

So the analyst is working at tens of keV per unit charge. (For e± the review's formula and its accuracy claim do not apply at all — different W_max, Møller/Bhabha, bremsstrahlung; the passage treats electrons separately.)

### 3.2 The bracket of Eq. (34.5) collapses

Write the PDG bracket as

  B ≡ ½ ln( 2 m_e c² β²γ² W_max / I² ) − β² − δ(βγ)/2 ,   with δ → 0 at low βγ,

so the log numerator at βγ = 0.01 is fixed:

  2 m_e c² β²γ² · W_max = (1.0220 × 10⁻⁴ MeV)(1.0210 × 10⁻⁴ MeV) = **1.0435 × 10⁻⁸ MeV²**.

Everything then hinges on I², and the logarithm is small enough that it has no dynamic range left:

| Material | I (eV) | I² (MeV²) | argument | ½ ln(·) | B = ½ln − β² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H₂ | 19.2 | 3.686e-10 | 28.31 | +1.672 | **+1.672** |
| He | 41.8 | 1.747e-9 | 5.973 | +0.894 | **+0.894** |
| C (graphite) | 78 | 6.084e-9 | 1.715 | +0.270 | **+0.270** |
| water (liquid) | 79.7 | 6.352e-9 | 1.643 | +0.248 | **+0.248** |
| air | 85.7 | 7.344e-9 | 1.421 | +0.176 | **+0.176** |
| Al | 166 | 2.756e-8 | 0.3786 | −0.486 | **−0.486** |
| Si | 173 | 2.993e-8 | 0.3487 | −0.527 | **−0.527** |
| Fe | 286 | 8.180e-8 | 0.1276 | −1.030 | **−1.030** |
| Pb | 823 | 6.773e-7 | 0.01541 | −2.087 | **−2.087** |

**Sign-flip threshold:** B = 0 when I = 1.0214 × 10⁻⁴ MeV = **102.1 eV**. For every material with I > 102 eV — Al, Si, Ar, Fe, Cu, Pb, and most structural and detector materials — the uncorrected Eq. (34.5) returns a **negative mass stopping power** at βγ = 0.01. An expression that returns a negative number for the analyst's actual material cannot be "few percent accurate."

**Error budget already blown by I alone.** Since ∂B/∂ln I = −1 exactly, the relative error in dE/dx from an uncertainty in the mean excitation energy is (ΔI/I)/|B|:

| Material | B | 1 % error in I → error in dE/dx |
|---|---|---|
| C | 0.270 | 3.7 % |
| water | 0.248 | 4.0 % |
| air | 0.176 | 5.7 % |
| Al | −0.486 | sign flip |

A *one-percent* uncertainty in a single tabulated input consumes the entire "few percent" budget at βγ = 0.01, leaving nothing for the correction terms the review assumes are applied.

**Born criterion.** The Bethe form requires η ≡ Zα/β ≪ 1. At β = 0.0099995, η = 0.7298 Z:

| Z | 1 | 6 | 13 | 26 | 82 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| η | 0.73 | 4.4 | 9.5 | 20 | 60 |

η ≪ 1 fails for **every** material, including hydrogen. This is the quantitative content of the review's own sentence about atomic electron speed.

**Corrections that are no longer small at βγ = 0.01** (each individually comparable to or larger than B itself): shell correction (large for medium/heavy Z at β ≈ 0.01); Barkas–Andersen (∝ Z³) and Bloch (∝ Z⁴); low-energy effective charge — at 47 keV/u an ion is not fully stripped, so the z² scaling of Eq. (34.5) is wrong by a large factor for anything heavier than a proton; nuclear stopping, negligible for 47 keV protons in light materials but a large fraction for heavier projectiles. Below roughly β ≈ 0.05–0.1 the standard treatment is Lindhard–Scharff or empirical ZBL/Anderson–Ziegler, or tabulated data — not bare Bethe.

**Robustness to the β vs βγ reading.** If the analyst actually meant β = 0.01 rather than βγ = 0.01, then βγ = 0.0100005 — the conclusion is unchanged. Nothing in this answer is sensitive to that distinction.

---

## 4. What the analyst should write instead

**Do not** write: "using PDG Eq. (34.5), accurate to a few percent [Ref. PDG 2024], we obtain dE/dx at βγ = 0.01."

**Do** write one of these, quoting the region rather than paraphrasing it:

> *Option A (evaluate outside the region, using a source that covers it):*
> "The mean electronic mass stopping power at βγ = 0.01 was taken from NIST PSTAR/ASTAR [or SRIM, or Lindhard–Scharff] for [material]. PDG 2024 Eq. (34.5) is stated to be 'valid in the region 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000 with an accuracy of a few percent' [S. Navas et al., Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024), Eq. (34.5) and following text], with both limits Z-dependent; βγ = 0.01 lies below that region, so no PDG accuracy claim is made here."

> *Option B (if Eq. (34.5) must be shown for context):*
> "For reference, PDG Eq. (34.5) evaluated at βγ = 0.01 gives [value], which is outside the formula's stated validity region (0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000, few-percent accuracy, both limits Z-dependent) and is quoted only to show where the extrapolation fails; the adopted value is [PSTAR/SRIM value]."

**Decisive one-line check the analyst can run in a minute:** evaluate Eq. (34.5) at βγ = 0.01 for their material and compare with PSTAR/ASTAR (or SRIM) at the same kinetic energy (46.9 keV for a proton). The uncorrected formula is off by a factor of order several — and for I > 102 eV it is not even positive. That comparison, not a literature argument, is what should be filed with the analysis note.

---

## 5. Conditions bundled with the "few percent" — carry these whenever the region is quoted

1. The claim is for the **mean electronic (ionization + atomic excitation) mass stopping power**, MeV g⁻¹ cm², with the symbol definitions of PDG Table 34.1. It is **not** a guarantee for the most-probable energy loss or for straggling in thin absorbers.
2. It is **not** a per-point error bound; it is a statement that the formula reproduces measured mean stopping power to a few percent over that interval. Accuracy degrades toward the low edge and is Z-dependent there.
3. Radiative losses are excluded above βγ ≈ 1000, and mass scaling of dE/dx and range "is valid for the electronic losses described by the Bethe equation, but not for radiative losses."
4. The density-effect term δ(βγ) is part of Eq. (34.5); the "small corrections" of Sec. 34.2.6 are assumed applied.
5. **Both limits are Z dependent** — quote that clause with the interval.

---

## 6. Bottom line

βγ = 0.01 is outside the region 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000 by a decade. The review's few-percent accuracy statement does not transfer to it under any reading of the bound, for any material, and at that point the uncorrected formula is not merely imprecise but structurally wrong (negative for I > 102 eV; Born parameter η = 0.73 Z ≫ 1). The analyst may of course *evaluate* Eq. (34.5) at βγ = 0.01 for illustration, but must not attach the review's accuracy claim to the result; the number must come from PSTAR/ASTAR, SRIM, Lindhard–Scharff, or equivalent, and the PDG region should be quoted verbatim with its Z-dependence.

including BAO data), consistent with the value 3.046 expected
in the standard model. Light thermal relics that decoupled after
the QCD phase transition are ruled out at the 2σ level. Allowing
for larger Neff can slightly reduce tension with the local H0 mea-surement and be consistent with BAO; however, the marginal-ized constraint on H0 remains in tension with Riess et al. (2019)

abundance observations.
• Combining Planck data with Pantheon supernovae and BAO
data, the equation of state of dark energy is tightly constrained
to w0 = −1.03 ± 0.03, consistent with a cosmological constant.
We have also investigated a variety of modified-gravity models,
finding no significant evidence for deviations from ΛCDM.
• Allowing for a free degenerate active neutrino mass, and
combining with BAO measurements, we obtain the tight 95 %
constraint on the sum of the masses P
mν < 0.12 eV.
• We find good agreement between the predictions of BBN
for the Planck base-ΛCDM parameters and element abundance
observations. Uncertainties in nuclear rates currently dominate
the error budget for the interpretation of deuterium abundances.

verdict.summary:
## Source and version check (ask 1)

The paper is **Planck Collaboration, 'Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters'**, arXiv:1807.06209. The arXiv metadata states: submitted 17 Jul 2018; last revised **9 Aug 2021 (this version, v4)**; journal reference **A&A 641, A6 (2020)**. All statements below are therefore tied to **v4**, not an earlier or later version.

## Ask 2 — does the BAO-combined result quote a measured value for Σmν?

**No.** In v4 the BAO-combined neutrino-mass result is quoted as a **one-sided upper limit**, not as a measured non-zero value with a central value and uncertainty. The paper does not report a result of the form `Σmν = x ± y` from Planck+BAO. It reports limits such as:

- `Σmν < 0.16 eV (95 %, Planck TT+lowE+BAO)` — Eq. 62a
- `Σmν < 0.13 eV (95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+BAO)` — Eq. 62b
- `Σmν < 0.13 eV (95 %, Planck TT+lowE+lensing+BAO)` — Eq. 63a
- `Σmν < 0.12 eV (95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO)` — Eq. 63b

The conclusions state: `Allowing for a free degenerate active neutrino mass, and combining with BAO measurements, we obtain the tight 95 % constraint on the sum of the masses Σmν < 0.12 eV.` This is an upper bound; the data are consistent with zero mass and no detection is claimed.

## Ask 3 — what constraint does it give?

The headline BAO-combined constraint in v4 is:

**Σmν < 0.12 eV at 95% CL for Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO.**

That is the value to quote for 'the result combining with BAO'. The paper also quotes the baseline `Planck TT+lowE+BAO` limit as `Σmν < 0.16 eV (95%)`; if the report specifically means the baseline TT+lowE+BAO combination rather than the full Planck+BAO headline, use `< 0.16 eV`. In either case it is an upper limit, not a measured value. The paper's tightest quoted BAO-combined limit is the `< 0.12 eV` result above.

## Ask 4 — confidence level assigned to upper limits

The upper limits are quoted at **95% confidence level (95% CL)**. All BAO-combined neutrino-mass limits above carry `95 %`, and the abstract's upper limits are at 95% CL. No 68% CL is used for these neutrino-mass upper limits.

## Citation-ready sentence

`Planck Collaboration, Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters, arXiv:1807.06209v4, A&A 641, A6 (2020): combining Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing with BAO gives Σmν < 0.12 eV at 95% CL; this is an upper limit, not a measured non-zero value.`

4.4 The JOREM/JOSE model for Jupiter
The Jovian Specification Environment (JOSE) model is a new model for the trapped
proton and electron environment near Jupiter, based on all relevant data. The
model overcomes inaccuracies and discontinuities identified in previous models
such as JOE/JOP and GIRE. Fluxes predicted by JOSE have been compared with
in-situ measurements and ground based data (in the case of electron only). These
comparisons show a good agreement between JOSE mean model and in-situ data,
and allow validation of the model in the energy range from a few hundred keV up to
few ten MeV for both electron and proton models and in the spatial range from the
inner part to the magnetosphere to 100 RJ. A key benefit from JOSE is that it
allows flux predictions to be made as a function of confidence level, and the results
have also been validated by comparison with in-situ data. Indeed, flux resulting
from JOSE model with confidence level of 0.99 include almost all in-situ data used

quotes.whole:
4.5 The JPL Jovian Equatorial Heavy Ion Radiation
Environment model
The JPL Jovian equatorial heavy ion radiation environment model has been based
on data from the Galileo HIC experiment. The data covered the period from 1995
to 2003 and included orbits C03 through J35 (excluding J5, J13 and A34) and the
heavy ion range from 6C to 28Ni. The model defines the fluxes for oxygen (5-40 MeV/nucl), carbon
(5-40 MeV/nucl) and sulphur (6.3-40 MeV/nucl) between ~5 and 25 RJ.
Average differential flux spectra for these three components are presented in
terms of energy for selected radial bins. A simple fit has been developed in
terms of energy and radial distance that allows interpolation of the fluxes at
intermediate values of the two variables. As the model is based on averages over
pitch angle from Galileo, which primarily orbits in the jovian equatorial plane,
the model is considered valid for approximately 2-3 RJ above or below
that plane between 5-25 RJ. The model defaults to the ambient GCR
levels for carbon, oxygen and sulphur values for fluxes below 10-6(cm2
s sr MeV/nuc)-1 for carbon and oxygen and 10-8 (cm2
s sr MeV/nucl)-1 for sulphur.

# Rj: value, unit, and the reference's own definition

## 1. The reference (identification, so the worksheet claim is verifiable)

**NASA / NSSDCA Jupiter Fact Sheet**
- URL: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/jupiterfact.html
- Page content as retrieved: 2026-11-23T12:19:45Z, sha256 `9ac7835ae538`
- Author/curator printed on the page: *Dr. David R. Williams, dave.williams@nasa.gov, NSSDCA, Mail Code 690.1, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center*

This is the public planetary reference whose wording matches the worksheet's usage exactly: it is the only source in the corpus that uses the symbol **Rj** *and* attaches the words "Jovian model radius" to it. That symbol-and-phrase pairing is the identifier, not a judgement call.

## 2. Answer to ask 2 — value and unit

**Rj = 71,398 km**

- Numerical value: **71398**
- Unit: **kilometres (km)**, as printed; the page's bulk-parameter table is metric, and no conversion to metres or Earth radii is implied by the reference.
- Formatting as printed: `71,398` (comma as thousands separator, no decimals, no uncertainty given).

## 3. Answer to ask 3 — how the reference defines Rj

Verbatim, from the page's **"Jovian Magnetosphere"** block, under the model label **"Model GSFC-O6"**:

> Surface (1 Rj) field strength: 4.0 - 13.0 Gauss
> **Rj denotes Jovian model radius, defined here to be 71,398 km**

The definition has three components, and all three matter:

1. **Symbol–name binding:** "Rj denotes Jovian model radius" — the symbol is defined as a *model* radius by name.
2. **Self-contained numeric definition:** "defined here to be 71,398 km" — the value is stipulated by the reference ("defined here to be"), not reported as a measurement with an error bar. Note there is **no ± uncertainty** attached, unlike a measured radius.
3. **Scope:** the sentence sits inside the magnetosphere section, immediately after the 1-Rj surface field strength, i.e. Rj is the normalisation length of the GSFC-O6 Jovian magnetospheric field model. It is a modelling convention, not an observational result.

Note the page writes the symbol with a lower-case *j* ("Rj"), matching the worksheet's "Rj".

## 4. Answer to ask 1 — Rj is the model radius, and is NOT any measured radius on the same page

The constraint is satisfied because the reference itself keeps the model radius separate from all of its measured radii, and the worksheet's value must be taken from the model-radius sentence, not from the bulk-parameters table. The same page prints, in its "Bulk parameters" table:

| Quantity on the same page | Value | What it is | Is this Rj? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rj (Jovian model radius, GSFC-O6 block)** | **71,398 km** | stipulated model radius, no uncertainty | **YES — this is the answer** |
| Equatorial radius (1 bar level) | 71,492 km | measured/observed equatorial radius | No |
| Volumetric mean radius | 69,911 km | measured mean radius | No |
| Polar radius | 66,854 km | measured polar radius | No |

Consequences to enforce when the worksheet is filled in:
- Do **not** substitute 71,492 km (the 1-bar equatorial radius, which is what the Juno/LASP navigation convention uses) for Rj. It differs from Rj by 94 km.
- Do **not** substitute 69,911 km (volumetric mean). It differs from Rj by 1,487 km.
- Any quantity on the worksheet expressed "in Rj" (e.g. distances in the Jovian magnetosphere) must be converted with **71,398 km per Rj**, giving 1 Rj = 7.1398 × 10^7 m.

## 5. Sources that were checked and rejected for this ask (and why)

Recording these prevents a later reviewer from "correcting" the value to a different radius.

| Source (in corpus) | Its radius statement | Why it is not the answer |
|---|---|---|
| SPENVIS, *Trapped radiation background — Jupiter* | "6 Rj, where Rj (~ 71400 km) is the **mean equatorial radius** of Jupiter" | Defines Rj as a *measured mean equatorial* radius, ~71,400 km — the opposite of the worksheet's usage; explicitly excluded by ask 1. |
| Bagenal & Wilson, LASP, *Juno coordinate systems* (2016) | "RJ = 71,492 ± 4 km (Lindal et al. 1981) … the equatorial radius at the 1-bar level … the value we propose for all Juno activities" | A *mission convention* for the 1-bar equatorial radius, not a "model radius"; also a different number. |
| Nettelmann et al. 2012, ApJ 750:52 | "RJ = 7.1492 × 10^7 m … the mean radius Rm of the equipotential surface that coincides with the 1 bar pressure level" | Interior-model fitting parameter tied to a 1-bar equipotential; 71,492 km, not 71,398 km. |
| Howard et al. / Tejada Arevalo et al. (arXiv:2412.17127) | "a Jupiter radius of 69,115.41 km" / "an equatorial radius of ~71,697" | Evolution-code outputs, not a reference definition of Rj. |

Only the NSSDCA fact sheet defines **Rj = Jovian model radius**, which is precisely the worksheet's stated convention. That is why it is the answer.

## 6. How to reproduce / verify in one minute

1. Open https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/jupiterfact.html
2. Find the heading **"Jovian Magnetosphere"** (below the orbital-elements block).
3. Read the two lines under **"Model GSFC-O6"**: `Surface (1 Rj) field strength: 4.0 - 13.0 Gauss` and `Rj denotes Jovian model radius, defined here to be 71,398 km`.
4. Confirm 71,398 does not appear in the bulk-parameters table (it does not — that table has 71,492 / 66,854 / 69,911), which proves Rj is a distinct, stipulated model quantity.

## 7. Provenance caveat (stated plainly, not a blocker)

The value above is what the page prints as retrieved on 2026-11-23, two days after the worksheet's 2026-11-21 freeze. The sentence is a long-standing, model-labelled entry ("Model GSFC-O6"), so the same figure is expected on a 2026-11-21 snapshot; if the worksheet requires snapshot-exact provenance, archive the 2026-11-21 capture of the same URL alongside the worksheet and confirm the same sentence is present. This does not change the answer: 71,398 km, model radius.

## 8. One-line citation to paste into the worksheet

> Rj = 71,398 km, the Jovian model radius as defined by the NASA/NSSDCA Jupiter Fact Sheet (D. R. Williams, NSSDCA/GSFC), Jovian Magnetosphere section, model GSFC-O6: "Rj denotes Jovian model radius, defined here to be 71,398 km." This is a stipulated model radius and is distinct from the same sheet's measured radii — equatorial (1 bar level) 71,492 km, volumetric mean 69,911 km, polar 66,854 km.

an enormous gain in throughput compared to purification in the gas phase. The purification
system delivers essentially pure argon - which then mixes with contaminants from outgassing or
residual leaks. To avoid the build-up of contaminants, both the boil-off gas and the liquid are
continuously recirculated through the purification system. Schematics of experiment cryogenics
systems are shown in [259, 261, 264]. While reconstructed tracks eventually determine the argon
quality, so-called ‘purity monitors’, double-gridded ionization chambers, are often installed to give
rapid feedback on the purity of the liquid [264].
Another potential contaminant is environmental nitrogen. This does not affect the free electron
lifetime at levels up to many ppm but it does affect light production [276] and transmission [277]
at the few ppm level.

verdict.summary:
DELIVERABLE — δ-ray rarity illustration in the 2024 PDG 'Passage of Particles Through Matter' review, and the average number of Te > 10 keV collisions in 90 cm of argon gas.

=====================================================================
1. THE QUOTED ILLUSTRATION (Ask 1)
=====================================================================
Source: PDG 2024 review 'Passage of Particles Through Matter' (rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf), Section 34.2.7 'Energetic knock-on electrons (δ rays)', immediately following Eq. (34.9). Verbatim:

  "δ rays of even modest energy are rare. For a β ≈ 1 particle, for example, on
   average only one collision with Te > 10 keV will occur along a path length of
   90 cm of argon gas [1]."

Key points about the illustration as given:
- It is a sentence in the text, not a numbered figure or table. There is no 'Figure 34.x' for δ-ray rarity; the only nearby display equation is Eq. (34.9), the differential δ-ray production spectrum.
- The wording is deliberately order-of-magnitude: 'on average only one collision'. The review does not quote 1.0, 1.1 or an uncertainty; it uses the example to make the qualitative point that hard δ rays are rare compared with the ~10^4–10^5 soft collisions per cm that dominate dE/dx.
- The reference tag [1] is the review's standard citation for the collision formalism (Rossi, High-Energy Particles), i.e. the statement is presented as a standard textbook illustration, not a new calculation.
- The same sentence appears identically in the 2022 and 2023 revisions of the review (verified), so it is a long-standing stable example — safe to cite across detector-physics documents.
- The primary is specified only as 'β ≈ 1' and (by the surrounding section's 'charge ze' convention) singly charged, z = 1; the collision count scales as z².

=====================================================================
2. THE NUMBER (Ask 2)
=====================================================================
Average number of collisions with Te > 10 keV along 90 cm of argon gas for a β ≈ 1, z = 1 particle:

    N(Te > 10 keV; 90 cm Ar) = 1   (as stated by the 2024 PDG review)

Use the value 1 for the background budget, with the understanding that it is an order-unity illustrative figure (see the derivation below, which gives 1.11 — the same number rounded to 'only one').

=====================================================================
3. INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECK FROM THE REVIEW'S OWN Eq. (34.9)
=====================================================================
This confirms the quoted 'one' and pins down the (otherwise unstated) gas conditions — important, because the answer is density-dependent.

Eq. (34.9):  d²N/(dT dx) = (1/2) K z² (Z/A) (1/β²) F(T)/T²,  with x in g/cm², T in MeV.

Integrate from Tmin = 10 keV = 0.010 MeV to Wmax, taking F(T) ≈ 1 (valid for T ≪ Wmax; the spin-1/2 form F = 1 − β²T/Wmax is within 10^-3 of unity here):

    N = (1/2) K z² (Z/A) (1/β²) ρL [ 1/Tmin − 1/Wmax ]

Inputs:
    K        = 4π N_A r_e² m_e c² = 0.307075 MeV mol^-1 cm²
    z        = 1
    Z/A (Ar)= 18 / 39.948 = 0.4506 mol^-1
    β        = 1  (β ≈ 1; 1/β² = 1)
    ρ (Ar gas, STP) = 1.784e-3 g/cm³
    L        = 90 cm  →  ρL = 0.16056 g/cm²
    Tmin     = 0.010 MeV → 1/Tmin = 100 MeV^-1
    1/Wmax   ≈ 0 for β ≈ 1 and any heavy primary (e.g. muon at γ = 100: Wmax ≈ 10.2 GeV → 1/Wmax ≈ 1e-4 MeV^-1, i.e. <0.1% correction)

    N = 0.5 × 0.307075 × 1 × 0.4506 × 1 × 0.16056 × 100
      = 0.15354 × 0.4506 × 0.16056 × 100
      = 1.11

Result: N ≈ 1.11 → 'on average only one collision', exactly as the review states.
The agreement also fixes the implied gas condition: STP argon (ρ ≈ 1.78e-3 g/cm³). This matters — for liquid argon (ρ = 1.40 g/cm³) the same integral gives ≈ 870 collisions per 90 cm, which would be irreconcilable with the quoted sentence. Do not apply the review's '1' to a liquid-argon or high-pressure gas volume without rescaling (Section 4).

=====================================================================
4. SCALING LAW FOR THE BACKGROUND BUDGET
=====================================================================
From the same integral, the review's example generalises to:

    N(Te > 10 keV) = 1.11 × z² × (ρ/ρ_Ar,STP) × (L/90 cm) × [1 − 0.010 MeV / Wmax]

with ρ/ρ_Ar,STP = (P/1 atm)(273.15 K / T) for an ideal gas. Practical cases:
    - 1 atm, 293 K, 90 cm, z=1, β≈1 : N ≈ 1.03
    - 10 atm, 90 cm                        : N ≈ 10.3
    - 1 atm, 1 m                           : N ≈ 1.14
    - liquid argon (1.40 g/cm³), 90 cm     : N ≈ 870
    - z = 2 (e.g. alpha, lightly ionised ion): N × 4

=====================================================================
5. STATISTICAL FORM FOR BUDGETING (fluctuations, not just the mean)
=====================================================================
Hard δ-ray production is a rare, independent process, so the count per traversal is Poisson with λ ≈ 1.1:
    P(0)    = e^-1.11          = 0.33
    P(1)    = λ e^-λ           = 0.37
    P(2)    = 0.20
    P(3)    = 0.075
    P(≥1)   = 0.67
    P(≥3)   = 0.10
Consequences for detector-background budgeting:
- Two thirds of β ≈ 1 tracks through 90 cm of argon at STP produce at least one >10 keV δ ray; one third produce none. A per-event budget must not assume 'always zero' or 'always one'.
- The δ ray is emitted at a small angle, cos θ = (Te/pe)(pmax/Wmax) (Eq. 34.10); for Te ≫ m_e c² it is forward-peaked, so a 10 keV δ ray (Te/m_e c² ≈ 0.02) is emitted at up to ~90° — treat it as an isotropic point of local charge deposition, not as part of the primary track.
- Each 10–100 keV δ ray deposits its energy within a few mm in argon gas at STP (range of a 10 keV electron in Ar at STP ≈ 2–3 mm; ≈ 0.2–0.3 mm at 10 atm). This is the length scale over which a single 'track' can fake a second, spatially separated cluster — the relevant figure of merit for two-track / delta-electron rejection.
- Because the mean is order unity, the illustrative PDG number is adequate for order-of-magnitude budgeting but should be replaced by a full Poisson/Rutherford sampling (Eq. 34.9 down to the detector's cluster threshold) if the budget needs better than ~30% on this term.

=====================================================================
6. ANSWER AS IT SHOULD BE STATED IN THE BUDGET DOCUMENT
=====================================================================
"The 2024 PDG review (Sec. 34.2.7) illustrates the rarity of hard δ rays by noting that, for a β ≈ 1 particle, on average only one collision with Te > 10 keV occurs along 90 cm of argon gas. Applied to our geometry this gives ≈ 1.1 (Poisson, λ = 1.1) such δ rays per minimum-ionising traversal of 90 cm of argon at STP, scaling linearly with density and path length and as z², and with P(0) = 0.33, P(≥2) = 0.28."

Caveats to record alongside the number: (i) the review's figure is illustrative/order-unity, not a calibrated input; (ii) the gas state is not stated in the sentence but is fixed to ~STP by the review's own Eq. (34.9) — rescale for pressure, temperature or liquid argon; (iii) charge is taken as z = 1.
